terms.text: 1. Text on an object that explains what that object does or can do. 2. An activated or triggered ability on the stack. This kind of ability is an object. See rule 113, “Abilities,” and section 6, “Spells, Abilities, and Effects.”
An italicized word with no rules meaning that ties together abilities on different cards that have similar functionality.
A kind of ability. Activated abilities are written as “[Cost]: [Effect.] [Activation instructions (if any).]” See rule 113, “Abilities,” and rule 602, “Activating Activated Abilities.”
Everything that appears before the colon in an activated ability’s text. It must be paid to activate the ability.
The player whose turn it is.

A system that determines the order by which players make choices if multiple players are instructed to make choices at the same time. This rule is modified for games using the shared team turns option; see rule 805.6.
The team whose turn it is in a game using the shared team turns option.
A cost a spell may have that its controller may pay (or, in some cases, must pay) in addition to its mana cost to cast that spell.
Cards with a two-part card frame (one part of which is inset on the left) on a single card where the alternative characteristics include the Adventure spell type.
A different name used on promotional or alternate-art versions of some cards. This name has no rules meaning.
A multiplayer variant played among two or more teams of equal size.
A cost a spell may have that its controller can pay rather than paying its mana cost.
A word that precedes one of two abilities a permanent may enter the battlefield with.
1. A zone used only when playing “for keeps.” 2. To put a card into the ante zone. See rule 407, “Ante.”
A spell or ability may require “any target.” “Any target” is the same as “target creature, player, planeswalker, or battle.”
See Active Player, Nonactive Player Order.
1. A casual variant in which a team of players faces off against a single opponent strengthened with powerful scheme cards. A player in an Archenemy game who is playing with a scheme deck.
A Commander game that follows a modified version of the Archenemy rules.
A card type. An artifact is a permanent.
A combination of artifact and creature that’s subject to the rules for both.
A combination of artifact and land that’s subject to the rules for both. Artifact lands can only be played as lands, not cast as spells.
A subtype that’s correlated to the artifact card type.
Text used to indicate that the game, for some specific purpose, treats a condition as true even though it’s not.
To determine how an attacking or blocking creature will deal its combat damage.

A trigger condition printed on abilities that triggered at the beginning of the end step (which is not the last thing to happen in the turn). Cards that were printed with that text have received errata in the Oracle card reference to say “at the beginning of the end step” or “at the beginning of the next end step.”
To send a creature into combat offensively. A creature can attack a player or a planeswalker.
A creature “attacks alone” if it’s the only creature declared as an attacker during the declare attackers step. A creature “is attacking alone” if it’s attacking but no other creatures are.
An option that may be used in certain multiplayer variants.
An option that may be used in certain multiplayer variants.
An option that may be used in certain multiplayer variants.

A creature that has either been declared as part of a legal attack during the combat phase (once all costs to attack, if any, have been paid), or a creature that has been put onto the battlefield attacking. It remains an attacking creature until it’s removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first.
The team who can attack during the combat phase of a multiplayer game using the shared team turns option.
An ability that triggers when a creature “attacks and isn’t blocked” triggers when the creature becomes an unblocked attacking creature.
An artifact type seen only on nontraditional Magic cards in the Unfinity expansion.
An optional deck of at least three (in limited play) or ten (in constructed play) Attraction cards that can be used to support play with some cards from the Unfinity expansion.
An enchantment subtype. Aura spells target objects or players, and Aura permanents are attached to objects or players.
An enchantment type that, in combination with the “choose a Background” ability, may allow a legendary enchantment card to be your commander.
Banding is a keyword ability that modifies the rules for declaring attackers and assigning combat damage. “Bands with other” is a specialized version of the ability.
Effects that change the base power and/or base toughness of a creature set one or both of those values to a specific number.
A supertype that’s normally relevant on lands. Any land with this supertype is a basic land.
There are five “basic land types”: Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, and Forest. Each one has a mana ability associated with it.
See Typecycling.
A card type. A battle is a permanent.
A zone. The battlefield is the zone in which permanents exist. It used to be known as the “in-play” zone.
A word used in some trigger events to indicate a change in status or characteristics.
Part of the turn. This step is the first step of the combat phase.
Part of the turn. This phase is the first phase of the turn.
To send a creature into combat defensively. A creature can block an attacking creature.
A creature “blocks alone” if it’s the only creature declared as a blocker during the declare blockers step. A creature “is blocking alone” if it’s blocking but no other creatures are.

An attacking creature that another creature blocks or that an effect causes to become blocked. It remains a blocked creature until it’s removed from combat, an effect says that it becomes unblocked, or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first.

A creature that has either been declared as part of a legal block during the combat phase (once all costs to block, if any, have been paid), or a creature that has been put onto the battlefield blocking. It remains a blocking creature until it’s removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first.
A Blood token is a colorless artifact token with “{1}, {T}, Discard a card, Sacrifice this token: Draw a card.” For more information about predefined tokens, see rule 111.10.
A group of unopened Magic cards from a particular expansion. Booster packs are used in Limited formats.
An option for the Commander casual variant.

A term that meant “put [a permanent] into its owner’s graveyard.” In general, cards that were printed with the term “bury” have received errata in the Oracle card reference to read, “Destroy [a permanent]. It can’t be regenerated,” or “Sacrifice [a permanent].”

The standard component of the game. Magic cards may be traditional or nontraditional. Tokens aren’t considered cards. In the text of spells or abilities, the term “card” is used only to refer to a card that’s not on the battlefield or on the stack, such as a creature card in a player’s hand.
In a Limited format, the cards a player may use, in addition to basic land cards, to build their deck.
A characteristic. Except for abilities on the stack, each object has a card type, even if that object isn’t a card. Each card type has its own rules.
An enchantment subtype. Cases have a “to solve” ability that set a condition its controller must meet in order for the “solved” ability to take effect.
An obsolete term that referred to the player who cast a spell. In general, cards that were printed with the term “caster” have received errata in the Oracle card reference to say “controller.”
An obsolete term for mana cost. Cards printed with this text have received errata in the Oracle card reference.

“Champion” is a keyword ability that lets one creature temporarily replace another. A permanent is “championed” by another permanent if the latter exiles the former as the direct result of a champion ability.
To choose a new, legal target for a spell or ability.
An ability of a plane card that triggers “Whenever chaos ensues” in the Planechase casual variant.
The chaos symbol appears on the planar die and near some triggered abilities of plane cards in the Planechase casual variant.

A kind of static ability that conveys information about an object’s characteristics that would normally be found elsewhere on that object (such as in its mana cost, type line, or power/toughness box).
Information that defines an object.

A variant of the partner ability that lets two legendary permanent cards be your commander in the Commander variant rather than one if one of them has the “choose a Background” ability and the other is a Background enchantment card.
A designation a player can have. The ascend keyword causes a player to get this designation once they control ten permanents.
An enchantment subtype. Classes have a number of class level abilities that increase their level and grant them new abilities.
Part of the turn. This step is the second and final step of the ending phase.
A Clue token is a colorless artifact token with “{2}, Sacrifice this token: Draw a card.” For more information about predefined tokens, see rule 111.10.
A number printed on most cards that has no effect on game play.
1. A characteristic of an object. An attribute mana may have.
A set of colors that determines what cards may be included in a deck for the Commander casual variant.
A characteristic of an object.
1. An object with no color is colorless. Colorless is not a color. A type of mana.
Damage dealt during the combat damage step by attacking creatures and blocking creatures as a consequence of combat.
Part of the turn. This step is the fourth step of the combat phase.
Part of the turn. This phase is the third phase of the turn.
A zone for certain specialized objects that have an overarching effect on the game, yet are not permanents and cannot be destroyed.
1. A casual variant in which each deck is led by a legendary card (usually a creature). A designation given to one legendary card in each player’s deck in the Commander casual variant.
A casual variant in which players participate in a booster draft and then play multiplayer games.
A variant of the ninjutsu ability.
Informal term for the additional cost to cast a commander based on the number of times a player has cast it previously this game.
To remove a dungeon card from the game after reaching that dungeon card’s bottommost room.
To quit the game. Conceding a game immediately causes that player to leave that game and lose that game.
A card type used in Limited formats such as Conspiracy Draft. A conspiracy card is not a permanent.
A casual variant in which players participate in a booster draft and then play multiplayer games.
A way of playing in which each player creates their own deck ahead of time.
An obsolete term that appeared on the type line of artifacts without activated abilities. Cards printed with this text have received errata in the Oracle card reference to simply say “Artifact.”
An effect that modifies characteristics of objects, modifies control of objects, or affects players or the rules of the game, for a fixed or indefinite period.
“Control” is the system that determines who gets to use an object in the game. An object’s “controller” is the player who currently controls it.
To make all choices and decisions that player is allowed to make, or is told to make, by rules or by any objects.
An obsolete term for mana value. Cards printed with this term have received errata in the Oracle card reference.
Values of an object’s characteristics that are checked by copy effects.
1. To create a new object whose copiable values have been set to those of another object. 2. An object whose copiable values have been set to those of another object. See rule 707, “Copying Objects.”
An action or payment necessary to take another action or to stop another action from taking place.

Some older cards were printed with text stating that the card “counts as” something. Cards printed with this text have received errata in the Oracle card reference to state that the card actually is that thing.
A card type. A creature is a permanent.
A subtype that’s correlated to the creature card type and the kindred card type.
Targeting an opponent, anything that opponent controls, and/or any cards in an opponent’s graveyard is a crime.
Objects can deal “damage” to creatures, planeswalkers, and players. This is generally detrimental to the object or player that receives that damage.

Previously, if a creature blocks or becomes blocked by multiple creatures, the creature’s controller would be required to choose an order in which it would assign combat damage to the creatures blocking or blocked by it. Now, its controller no longer needs to assign an order, and simply divides its combat damage as they choose among all creatures it’s blocking or blocked by.
Along with night, a designation the game can have.
An ability found on the front faces of some double-faced cards. Cards with daybound and nightbound are face up when it’s day and face down when it’s night.
See Damage.
The collection of cards a player starts the game with; it becomes that player’s library.

To choose a set of creatures that will attack, declare whether each creature is attacking the defending player or a planeswalker that player controls, and pay any costs required to allow those creatures to attack.
Part of the turn. This step is the second step of the combat phase.
To choose a set of creatures that will block, declare which attacking creature each creature is blocking, and pay any costs required to allow those creatures to block.
Part of the turn. This step is the third step of the combat phase.

The player who can be attacked, and whose planeswalkers can be attacked, during the combat phase. In certain multiplayer games, there may be more than one defending player; see rule 802, “Attack Multiple Players Option,” and rule 805.10.
The team who can be attacked, and whose planeswalkers can be attacked, during the combat phase of a multiplayer game using the shared team turns option.
1. Part of a card that only battle cards have. A battle card’s defense is printed in its lower right corner. 2. A characteristic that only battles can have.
An ability created by effects generated when some spells or abilities resolve, or when some replacement effects are applied, that does something later on rather than at that time.
A system that may be used to determine in which order continuous effects in the same layer or sublayer are applied.
An option that may be used in certain multiplayer variants to pass control of creatures between teammates.
A numerical value a player has, equal to the number of mana symbols of a certain color among the mana costs of permanents that player controls.
A creature or planeswalker “dies” if it is put into a graveyard from the battlefield.

A partner ability that allows a player to play with two legendary creature cards as their commander if one of them has Doctor’s companion and the other is a Time Lord Doctor with no other creature types.
A door is one half of a Room permanent.
A variant of the hidden agenda ability.
Cards with two faces, one on each side of the card, and no Magic card back.

1. A Limited format in which players choose cards one at a time from booster packs, then construct a deck solely from the chosen cards and basic land cards. 2. To choose a card during a draft and put it into your card pool.
Part of a draft in which each player opens an unopened booster pack and the cards in those booster packs are drafted.

1. To put the top card of a player’s library into their hand as a turn-based action or as the result of an effect that uses the word “draw.” The result of a game in which neither player wins or loses.
Part of the turn. This step is the third and final step of the beginning phase.
A card type found on nontraditional Magic cards. A dungeon card is not a permanent.

Some older cards used the phrase “during [phase], [action].” These abilities were called “phase abilities.” In general, cards that were printed with phase abilities have received errata in the Oracle card reference so they have abilities that trigger at the beginning of a step or phase. “During” still appears in current card text, but only in its normal English sense and not as game terminology.
An older name for the Commander casual variant.
Something that happens in the game as a result of a spell or ability.
An emblem is a marker used to represent an object that has one or more abilities, but no other characteristics.
The middle player on each team in an Emperor game.
A multiplayer variant played among three-player teams.
A card type. An enchantment is a permanent.
A subtype that’s correlated to the enchantment card type.
A term that describes the relationship between a permanent and a card exiled by a cipher ability.
To move a phenomenon card off the top of a planar deck and turn it face up.
Part of the turn. This step is the fifth and final step of the combat phase.
Part of the turn. This step is the first step of the ending phase.
To “end the combat phase” as the result of an effect is to perform an expedited process that skips everything else that would happen that phase.
To “end the turn” as the result of an effect is to perform an expedited process that skips nearly everything else that would happen that turn.
Part of the turn. This phase is the fifth and final phase of the turn.
A designation a player can have. The storied keyword causes a player to get this designation once they control three permanents that are artifacts, Sagas, and/or legendary.
The energy symbol {E} represents one energy counter. To pay {E}, a player removes one energy counter from themselves.
In rules text, to enter the battlefield. See “Enters the Battlefield.”

A nontoken permanent enters the battlefield when it’s moved onto the battlefield from another zone. A token enters the battlefield as it’s created. This phrase has been shortened to simply “enters” in rules text on cards in most contexts.
An artifact subtype. Equipment can be attached to creatures.
An ability that restricts what creatures can block an attacking creature.
Anything that happens in a game.
Damage dealt to a creature greater than what would be lethal damage or damage dealt to a planeswalker greater than its loyalty.
A card’s expansion symbol is a small icon normally printed below the right edge of the illustration that has no effect on game play.
A word found on some abilities that care how much mana a player has spent to cast spells this turn.

A turn created by an effect of a spell or ability. For rules about extra turns in a multiplayer game using the shared team turns option, see 805.8. For rules about extra turns in a Grand Melee game, see rule 807.4.

1. A card is “face down” if it’s physically positioned so the card back is showing. Cards in some zones are normally kept face down. See section 4, “Zones.” 2. A status a permanent may have. Face-down spells have additional rules.
1. A card is “face up” if it’s physically positioned so the card front is showing. Cards in some zones are normally kept face up. See section 4, “Zones.” 2. A default status a permanent may have.
A counter that exiles the permanent it is on if that permanent would go to the graveyard from the battlefield.
Text in italics (but not in parentheses) in the text box of a card that has no effect on play.
An italicized word with no rules meaning that provides a flavorful description of an ability.
Cards with a two-part card frame (one part of which is printed upside down) on a single card.
A status a permanent may have.
A method of randomization with two possible outcomes of equal likelihood.
A Food token is a colorless artifact token with “{2}, {T}, Sacrifice this token: You gain 3 life.” For more information about predefined tokens, see rule 111.10.
One of the five basic land types. Any land with this subtype has the ability “{T}: Add {G}.”
See Typecycling.
See Landwalk.
A card exiled using the foretell special action becomes foretold. Other effects can also make an exiled card foretold. A spell was foretold if it was a foretold card in exile before it was cast.
An artifact subtype. Fortifications can be attached to lands.
A multiplayer variant in which a group of players compete as individuals against each other.
A player has a full party if the number of creatures in their party is four.
A split card on the stack that has been cast using the fuse ability or a copy of such a card.
Any player in the Emperor multiplayer variant who isn’t an emperor.
Mana in a cost represented by numerical symbols (such as {1}) or variable symbols (such as {X}) that can be paid with mana of any type.
An obsolete term for a non-Aura enchantment. Cards printed with this text have received errata in the Oracle card reference.
A designation a permanent can have. Goaded creatures are forced to attack and to attack a player other than the player that caused it to be goaded.
A Gold token is a colorless artifact token with “Sacrifice this token: Add one mana of any color.” For more information on predefined tokens, see rule 111.10.
A multiplayer variant in which a large group of players (usually ten or more) compete as individuals against each other.
1. A zone. A player’s graveyard is their discard pile. 2. All the cards in a player’s graveyard. See rule 404, “Graveyard.”
1. A zone. A player’s hand is where that player holds cards they have drawn but not played yet. 2. All the cards in a player’s hand. See rule 402, “Hand.”
A characteristic that only vanguards have.
A designation permanents can have. Infinity permanents have their ∞ abilities as long as they are harnessed.
A Heartwood token is a red and green artifact token with “{T}: Add {R} or {G}.” For more information about predefined tokens, see rule 111.10.
A zone in which not all players can be expected to see the cards’ faces.
An object is historic if it has the legendary supertype, the artifact card type, or the Saga subtype.
A counter on an Equipment that gives the equipped creature +1/+0.
A card with one or more hybrid mana symbols in its mana cost.
A mana symbol that represents a cost that can be paid in one of two ways.
A mana symbol that represents a cost that can be paid in one of three ways.

A Junk token is a colorless artifact token with {T}, Sacrifice this token: Exile the top card of your library. You may play that card this turn. Activate only as a sorcery.” For more information about predefined tokens, see rule 111.10.
See Intervening “If” Clause.
An action that violates the rules of the game and/or requirements or restrictions created by effects.
A target that no longer exists or no longer meets the specifications stated by the spell or ability that’s targeting it.
A picture printed on the upper half of a card that has no effect on game play.
Information printed directly below the text box that has no effect on game play.
“Imprint” used to be a keyword ability. It is now an ability word and has no rules meaning. All cards printed with the imprint keyword have received errata in the Oracle card reference.

An obsolete term for the battlefield. Cards that were printed with text that contain the phrases “in play,” “from play,” “into play,” or the like are referring to the battlefield and have received errata in the Oracle card reference. See Battlefield.

An instant spell that’s been cast, or an activated ability that’s been activated, while another spell or ability is on the stack has been cast or activated “in response to” the earlier spell or ability.

An Incubator token is a double-faced token. Its front face is a colorless Incubator artifact with “{2}: Transform this token.” Its back face is a 0/0 colorless Phyrexian artifact creature named “Phyrexian Token.” For more information about predefined tokens, see rule 111.10.
See Dependency.
1. An artifact subtype. 2. ∞ is a keyword found on Infinity cards that grants an ability as long as that permanent is harnessed.

A designation a player can have. Some effects instruct a player to take the initiative. The player with the initiative ventures into Undercity whenever they take the initiative and at the beginning of their upkeep.
A card type. An instant is not a permanent.
Effects that use the word “instead” are replacement effects. The word “instead” indicates what an event will be replaced with.

An obsolete card type. All cards printed with this card type are now instants. All abilities that, as printed, said a player could “play as an interrupt” can now be activated like any other activated abilities (unless they’re mana abilities, in which case they follow those rules instead). All relevant cards have been given errata in the Oracle card reference.
A specially worded condition checked as a triggered ability would trigger and again as it would resolve.
One of the five basic land types. Any land with this subtype has the ability “{T}: Add {U}.”
See Typecycling.

An obsolete keyword ability that meant “This creature can’t attack unless defending player controls an Island” and “When you control no Islands, sacrifice this creature.” Cards printed with this ability have been given errata in the Oracle card reference.
See Landwalk.
A game term, such as “flying” or “haste,” used as shorthand for a longer ability or group of abilities.
A verb, such as “destroy” or “cast,” used as a game term rather than as its normal English meaning.
A marker placed on an object that modifies its characteristics by granting it a keyword.
Kicker is a keyword ability that represents an optional additional cost. A spell has been kicked if its controller declared the intention to pay any or all of its kicker costs.
A card type. Whether or not a kindred is a permanent depends on its other card type.
A card type. A land is a permanent.
A subtype that’s correlated to the land card type.

A Lander token is a colorless artifact token with “{2}, {T}, Sacrifice this token: Search your library for a basic land card, put it onto the battlefield tapped, then shuffle.” For more information about predefined tokens, see rule 111.10.

Information about an object that’s no longer in the zone it’s expected to be in, or information about a player who’s no longer in the game. This information captures that object’s last existence in that zone or that player’s last existence in the game.
A system used to determine in which order continuous effects are applied.
A permanent “leaves the battlefield” when it’s moved from the battlefield to another zone, or (if it’s phased in) when it leaves the game because its owner leaves the game.
Information printed directly below the text box that has no effect on game play.
An obsolete creature type. Cards printed with this subtype have been given errata in the Oracle card reference so they have the legendary supertype instead. See Legendary.
A state-based action that causes a player who controls two or more legendary permanents with the same name to put all but one into their owners’ graveyards.
A supertype that’s normally relevant on permanents.
An amount of damage greater than or equal to a creature’s toughness.
A numerical designation a permanent may have. A Class enchantment’s level determines what other abilities it has.
A symbol that represents a keyword ability indicating abilities, power, and toughness a leveler card may have.
Cards with striated text boxes and three power/toughness boxes.
1. A zone. A player’s library is where that player draws cards from. 2. All the cards in a player’s library. See rule 401, “Library.”
Each player has an amount of “life,” represented by that player’s “life total.” Life may be gained or lost.
A characteristic that only vanguards have.
A way of playing in which each player gets a quantity of unopened Magic product and creates their own deck on the spot.
An optional rule used in some multiplayer games that limits what a player can affect.
Two abilities printed on the same object such that one of them causes actions to be taken or objects to be affected and the other one directly refers to those actions or objects.
An obsolete term for an Aura. Cards printed with this text have received errata in the Oracle card reference.
To remove an unlocked designation from a permanent that has one or more unlocked halves.
One half of a split permanent is “locked” if it doesn’t have the appropriate unlocked designation.
Informal term for the current system of mulligan rules.
A set of actions that could be repeated indefinitely.
There are several ways to lose the game.
1. Part of a card that only planeswalker cards have. A planeswalker card’s loyalty is printed in its lower right corner. A characteristic that only planeswalkers have.
An activated ability with a loyalty symbol in its cost.
The game in which a spell (or ability) that created a subgame was cast (or activated).
Part of the turn. The first, or precombat, main phase is the second phase of the turn. The second, or postcombat, main phase is the fourth phase of the turn.
The primary resource in the game. It is spent to pay costs, usually when casting spells and activating abilities.
An activated or triggered ability that could create mana and doesn’t use the stack.
Older versions of the rules stated that unspent mana caused a player to lose life; this was called “mana burn.” That rule no longer exists.
A characteristic, and part of a card. A card’s mana cost is indicated by the mana symbols printed in its upper right corner.
Where mana created by an effect is temporarily stored.

An obsolete card type. All cards printed with this card type are now instants. All abilities that, as printed, said a player could “play as a mana source” are now mana abilities. All relevant cards have been given errata in the Oracle card reference.
An icon that represents mana or a mana cost.
The total amount of mana in a mana cost, regardless of color.

A Map token is a colorless Map artifact token with “{1}, {T}, Sacrifice this token: Target creature you control explores. Activate only as a sorcery.” For more information about predefined tokens, see rule 111.10.
A multiplayer game or a two-player series of games (usually best-two-of-three) played in a tournament.
The number of cards in hand a player must discard down to during their cleanup step.
A variant of the morph ability that puts a +1/+1 counter on the creature as it turns face up.
Cards with a Magic card face on one side and half of an oversized Magic card face on the other.
A card or token may merge with a permanent to form a merged permanent. This merged permanent is represented by more than one card and/or token.
If a rule or effect states that a player’s deck must contain at least a specific number of cards, that number is the player’s minimum deck size.
A spell or ability is “modal” if it has two or more options in a bulleted list preceded by instructions for a player to choose a number of those options, such as “Choose one —.”
One kind of double-faced card. Modal double-faced cards can be played with either of their two faces up.
A modified creature is a creature that has a counter on it, is equipped, or is enchanted by an Aura its controller also controls.

A designation a player can have. Some effects instruct a player to become the monarch. The monarch draws a card at the beginning of their end step. Dealing combat damage to the monarch steals the title from that player.

An obsolete term that appeared on the type line of artifacts with activated abilities that caused the artifact to become tapped as a cost. Cards printed with this text have received errata in the Oracle card reference to simply say “Artifact,” and those abilities now include the tap symbol in their costs.
An object with exactly one color is monocolored. Colorless objects aren’t monocolored.
See Hybrid Mana Symbols.
A designation given to a creature whose ability including a monstrosity instruction has resolved.
One of the five basic land types. Any land with this subtype has the ability “{T}: Add {R}.”
See Typecycling.
See Landwalk.

To remove a counter from one object and put it on a different object. Some older cards used “move” with respect to Auras; those cards have received errata in the Oracle card reference and now use the word “attach.”
To take a mulligan is to reject a prospective opening hand in favor of a new one.
An object with two or more colors is multicolored. Multicolored is not a color.
Multikicker is a variant of the kicker keyword ability. It represents an optional additional cost that may be paid any number of times.
A game that begins with more than two players. See section 8, “Multiplayer Rules.”

A creature spell cast using the mutate keyword ability. As it resolves, if its target creature is legal, it merges with the target creature. The resulting creature has all characteristics of the topmost component and has the abilities of each component.
A characteristic, and part of a card. A card’s name is printed in its upper left corner.
Along with day, a designation the game can have.
An ability found on the back faces of some double-faced cards. Cards with daybound and nightbound are face up when it’s day and face down when it’s night.
Any land that doesn’t have the supertype “basic.”
One kind of double-faced card. Nonmodal double-faced cards default to being cast with their front faces up but can transform to their back faces in some way.
A card not included in players’ decks. It may be oversized or have a card back other than a “Deckmaster” back.
An ability on the stack, a card, a copy of a card, an emblem, a token, a spell, or a permanent.
Cards with a two-part card frame (one part of which is inset on the left) on a single card where the alternative characteristics include the Omen spell type.
An effect that does something just once and doesn’t have a duration.
A supertype that appears only on scheme cards.
The hand of cards a player starts the game with, once the player has decided not to take any further mulligans.
Someone a player is playing against.
An additional rule or set of rules that can be used in a multiplayer game.
The reference that contains the up-to-date wordings (in English) for all tournament-legal cards. A card’s Oracle text can be found using the Gatherer card database at Gatherer.Wizards.com.
An object is “outside the game” if it isn’t in any of the game’s zones.
The player who (for purposes of the game) a card, permanent, token, or spell belongs to.
A term that describes a creature that’s been affected by a soulbond ability.

A keyword ability that lets two legendary cards be your commander in the Commander variant rather than one. “Partner with [name]” is a specialized version of the ability that works even outside of the Commander variant to help two cards reach the battlefield together.
Some cards refer to the number of creatures in your party. A player’s party includes up to one each of Cleric, Rogue, Warrior, and Wizard.
To decline to take any action (such as casting a spell or activating an ability) when you have priority.
All players “pass in succession” if each player in the game (starting with any one of them) opts not to take an action upon receiving priority.
A symbol shaped like a pawprint that is used to indicate the modes on some modal spells.
To perform the actions required by a cost. This often means, but is not restricted to, spending resources such as mana or life.
A card or token on the battlefield.
A card that could be put onto the battlefield.
A spell that will enter the battlefield as a permanent as part of its resolution.

An obsolete term used to indicate that a continuous effect has no duration and thus lasts until the end of the game. Cards printed with this term have received errata in the Oracle card reference to delete it.

1. A subsection of a turn. See section 5, “Turn Structure.” 2. A permanent “phases in” when its status changes from phased out to phased in. A permanent “phases out” when its status changes from phased in to phased out.
A status a permanent may have. Phased-in is the default status. Phased-out permanents are treated as though they do not exist. (“Phased-out” was a zone in older versions of the rules.)
A card type seen only on nontraditional Magic cards in the Planechase casual variant. A phenomenon card is not a permanent.
A mana symbol that represents a cost that can be paid either by spending colored mana or by paying life.
A symbol used in rules text to represent any of the five Phyrexian mana symbols.
A temporary grouping of cards.

(Obsolete) Some spells and abilities previously referred to a counter being “placed” on a permanent. These cards have received errata in the Oracle card reference to use the term “put” instead. Due to a rules change, these cards continue to function as they did before.
One of the five basic land types. Any land with this subtype has the ability “{T}: Add {W}.”
See Typecycling.
See Landwalk.
A deck of at least ten plane cards needed to play the Planechase casual variant.
A specialized six-sided die needed to play the Planechase casual variant.
A card type seen only on nontraditional Magic cards in the Planechase casual variant. A plane card is not a permanent.
A casual variant in which plane cards and phenomenon cards add additional abilities and randomness to the game.
A card type. A planeswalker is a permanent.
The Planeswalker symbol appears on the planar die in the Planechase casual variant.
A subtype that’s correlated to the planeswalker card type.

Older versions of the rules stated that a player who controlled two or more planeswalkers with the same planeswalker type would put all but one of those planeswalkers into their owners’ graveyards. This rule was called the “planeswalker uniqueness rule” and no longer exists.
One of the people in the game.
A card exiled using the plot special action becomes plotted. Other effects can also make an exiled card plotted.
A counter that may be given to a player.
Having one or more poison counters.

An obsolete term that appeared on the type line of artifacts with activated abilities that didn’t cause the artifact to be tapped as a cost. Cards printed with this text have received errata in the Oracle card reference to simply say “Artifact.”
A main phase that occurs after a combat phase. See Main Phase.
1. Part of a card that only creature cards have. A creature card’s power is printed before the slash in its lower right corner. A characteristic that only creatures have.
A Powerstone token is a colorless artifact token with “{T}: Add {C}. This mana can’t be spent to cast a nonartifact spell.” For more information about predefined tokens, see rule 111.10.
The first main phase of a turn. See Main Phase.
Cards with a two-part card frame (one part of which is inset on the right) on a single card.
The inset frame of a preparation card that includes its alternative characteristics.
A designation a permanent may have that allows you to cast a copy of that card with its alternative characteristics.
A word used by prevention effects to indicate what damage will not be dealt.
A kind of continuous effect that watches for a damage event that would happen and completely or partially prevents the damage that would be dealt.
Which player can take actions at any given time is determined by a system of “priority.”
An additional reward for visiting some Attractions.
Each battle has a player designated as its protector, and that player protects that battle.
Cards with a two-part card frame (one part of which is inset under the type line) on a single card.
A zone in which all players can be expected to see the cards’ faces.

A type of counter a player can have that causes that player to mill cards at the beginning of their precombat main phase, then lose 1 life and remove one rad counter for each nonland card milled this way.
See Limited Range of Influence.

Some older cards were printed with the term “redirect” to indicate a redirection effect. Such cards have received errata in the Oracle card reference so they explicitly state that damage that would be dealt to one object or player is dealt “instead” to another. See Redirection Effect.
A kind of replacement effect that causes damage that would be dealt to one creature, planeswalker, or player to be dealt instead to another creature, planeswalker, or player.
An ability that triggers based on actions taken earlier during a spell or ability’s resolution.
Parenthetical text in italics in the text box of a card that summarizes a rule that applies to that card, but is not actually rules text and has no effect on play.

Certain events can cause an attacking or blocking creature, or a planeswalker that’s being attacked, to be “removed from combat.” A permanent that’s removed from combat has no further involvement in that combat phase.

terms.term: Remove from the Game, Removed, Removed-from-the-Game Zone (Obsolete)
terms.text: “Remove [something] from the game” is an obsolete term for “exile [something].” “The removed card” is an obsolete term for “the exiled card.” The removed-from-the-game zone is an obsolete term for the exile zone. Cards with that text have received errata in the Oracle card reference. See Exile.
A designation given to a permanent as a result of the renown ability.
A kind of continuous effect that watches for a particular event that would happen and completely or partially replaces that event with a different event.
An effect that forces one or more creatures to attack or block.
When the spell or ability on top of the stack “resolves,” its instructions are followed and it has its effect.
To cast an instant spell or activate an ability while another spell or ability is already on the stack.
To immediately end the current game and restart it.
An effect that precludes one or more creatures from attacking or blocking.
An emblem that may be created at the time the Ring tempts you.
A designation that a creature can be given as the Ring tempts you.

Roles are colorless enchantment tokens. Each one has the Aura and Role subtypes and the enchant creature ability. If a permanent has more than one Role attached to it controlled by the same player, each of those Roles except the one with the most recent timestamp is put into its owner’s graveyard.
To roll a twenty-sided die. Similarly, a d4 is a four-sided die, a d6 is a six-sided die, and so on.
1. A subsection of a dungeon card. 2. An enchantment subtype found on some split cards.
A triggered ability that triggers whenever a player moves their venture marker into a room of a dungeon card.
A characteristic that defines a card’s abilities.
A designation given to a creature whose saddle ability has resolved.
An enchantment subtype. Sagas have a number of chapter abilities that take effect over a number of turns to tell a story.
A card type seen only on nontraditional Magic cards in the Archenemy casual variant. A scheme card is not a permanent.
A deck of at least twenty scheme cards needed to play the Archenemy casual variant.
A smaller name line with the Oracle reference name of a card which has an alternate name in its upper left corner.
“Set [something] aside” is an obsolete term for “exile [something].” Cards with that text have received errata in the Oracle card reference. See Exile.
A Shard token is a colorless enchantment token with “{2}, Sacrifice this token: Scry 1, then draw a card.” For more information on predefined tokens, see rule 111.10.
In the Two-Headed Giant multiplayer variant, each team has a “shared life total” rather than each player having an individual life total.
An option that may be used in certain multiplayer variants, such as Two-Headed Giant and Archenemy.
A counter that protects a permanent from being damaged or destroyed.
A mutually understood way for the game to advance forward a number of game choices (either taking an action or passing priority) without players needing to explicitly identify each such choice.
Extra cards that may be used to modify a deck between games of a match.

A battle subtype. Only an opponent of a Siege’s controller can be its protector. When the last defense counter is removed, its controller exiles the Siege, then they may cast it transformed without paying its mana cost.

Cards in certain sets and certain promotional cards are printed with a silver border. Silver-bordered cards are intended for casual play and may have features and text that aren’t covered by these rules.
Effects that use the word “skip” are replacement effects. The word “skip” indicates what events, steps, phases, or turns will be replaced with nothing.
See Typecycling.
A supertype that’s normally relevant on permanents.
The snow mana symbol {S} represents a cost that can be paid with one mana produced by a snow source. It can also represent mana from a snow source that was spent to pay a cost.

Some older cards were printed with the term “snow-covered” in their rules text. Except when referencing card names, such cards have received errata in the Oracle card reference to reference the supertype “snow” instead. See Snow.
A card type. A sorcery is not a permanent.
The object that generated that ability.
The object that dealt that damage.
The spell that produced mana or the source of the ability that produced mana.
An action a player may take that doesn’t use the stack.
Speed is a value that a player can have.
A card on the stack. Also a copy (of either a card or another spell) on the stack.
A kind of ability. Spell abilities are abilities that are followed as instructions while an instant or sorcery spell is resolving.
A subtype that’s correlated to the instant card type and the sorcery card type.
Cards with two card faces on a single card.
A zone. The stack is the zone in which spells, activated abilities, and triggered abilities wait to resolve.
After a player has set aside their sideboard, their remaining deck becomes their starting deck.
The number of cards a player draws as a game begins. In most games, each player’s starting hand size is seven.
The amount of life a player has as a game begins. In most games, each player’s starting life total is 20.
The player chosen to take the first turn of a game.
The team chosen to take the first turn of a game using the shared team turns option.
A triggered ability that triggers when a game state is true rather than triggering when an event occurs.
Game actions that happen automatically whenever certain conditions are met.
A kind of ability. Static abilities do something all the time rather than being activated or triggered.
Cards with striated text boxes, one or more station symbols, and the station ability.
The physical state of a permanent.
A subsection of a phase. See section 5, “Turn Structure.”
A marker placed on an object that modifies its characteristics or interacts with a rule or effect.
A kicker variant that can add a sticker to the spell with the ability and give a player a ticket counter.
The collection of stickers found on an insert in Unfinity booster packs.
A counter that stops a permanent from untapping.
A completely separate Magic game created by an effect.
A game supplement with a Magic card back that can be used to represent a double-faced card or meld card.
A characteristic that appears after the card type and a long dash on a card’s type line.

A term that was printed on some older cards. In general, cards that referred to a spell being “successfully cast” have received errata in the Oracle card reference to simply refer to a spell being “cast.”

Older creature cards were printed with “Summon [creature type]” on their type lines. All such cards have received errata in the Oracle card reference to say “Creature — [creature type].” (Many of these cards’ creature types have also been updated.) See Creature.

Informal term for a player’s inability to attack with a creature or to activate its abilities that include the tap symbol or the untap symbol unless the creature has been under that player’s control since the beginning of that player’s most recent turn.
A characteristic that appears before the card type on a card’s type line. Most cards don’t have a supertype.
A Free-for-All game in which each player is an archenemy.
One of the five basic land types. Any land with this subtype has the ability “{T}: Add {B}.”
See Typecycling.
See Landwalk.
To turn a permanent sideways from an upright position.
The tap symbol {T} in an activation cost means “Tap this permanent.”
A status a permanent may have.
A preselected object or player a spell or ability will affect.
A group of players who share a common victory condition in a multiplayer game.
A multiplayer variant played among two or more teams, each of which sits together.
In a multiplayer game between teams, a player’s teammates are the other players on their team.
Part of a card. The text box is printed on the lower half of the card and contains the card’s rules text, reminder text, and flavor text.
A continuous effect that changes the text that appears in an object’s text box and/or type line.
“Threshold” used to be a keyword ability. It is now an ability word and has no rules meaning. All cards printed with the threshold keyword have received errata in the Oracle card reference.

The ticket symbol {TK} with no numbers in it represents one ticket counter. The ticket symbol with a number in it represents a ticket cost. To pay a ticket cost, a player removes that many ticket counters from themselves.
A system used to determine in which order continuous effects in the same layer or sublayer are applied.
A marker used to represent any permanent that isn’t represented by a card.
An icon that appears in the upper left of some Odyssey block cards that has no effect on game play.
An obsolete term for mana value. Cards printed with this term have received errata in the Oracle card reference.

What a player actually has to pay, in practical terms, to cast a spell or activated ability: the mana cost, activation cost, or alternative cost, plus all cost increases (including additional costs) and minus all cost reductions.
An obsolete keyword ability that has been renamed.
1. Part of a card that only creature cards have. A creature card’s toughness is printed after the slash in its lower right corner. A characteristic that only creatures have.
An organized play activity where players compete against other players.
Additional rules that apply to games played in a sanctioned tournament.
A Magic card that measures approximately 2.5 inches (6.3 centimeters) by 3.5 inches (8.8 centimeters) and is included in players’ decks.
A variant of trample that modifies how a creature assigns combat damage if it’s attacking a planeswalker.
An older name for nonmodal double-faced cards.
A Treasure token is a colorless artifact token with “{T}, Sacrifice this token: Add one mana of any color.” For more information about predefined tokens, see rule 111.10.
An obsolete card type that has been renamed.

Whenever a game event or game state matches a triggered ability’s trigger event, that ability automatically “triggers.” That means its controller puts it on the stack the next time a player would receive priority.
The first part of a triggered ability, consisting of “when,” “whenever,” or “at” followed by a trigger event.
The event that a triggered ability looks for. Whenever the trigger event occurs, the triggered ability triggers.
A kind of ability. Triggered abilities begin with the word “when,” “whenever,” or “at.” They’re written as “[Trigger condition], [effect].”
Markers used to keep track of which players are taking turns in a Grand Melee game.
Game actions that happen automatically when certain steps or phases begin, or when each step or phase ends.
A multiplayer variant played among two-player teams that each have a shared life total and take a simultaneous turn.
1. An object’s card type or, more broadly, its card type, subtype, and/or supertype. An attribute mana has.
An icon that appears in the upper left of some Future Sight cards that has no effect on game play.
Part of a card. The type line is printed directly below the illustration and contains the card’s card type(s), subtype(s), and/or supertype(s).
An effect that changes an object’s card type, subtype, and/or supertype.
A variant of the cycling ability.
To move an Equipment away from the creature it’s attached to so that the Equipment is on the battlefield but is not equipping anything.
A term that meant “can’t be blocked.” Cards that used this term have received errata in the Oracle card reference.

An attacking creature once no creature has been declared as a blocker for it, unless an effect has caused it to become blocked. It remains an unblocked creature until it’s removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first.
A default status a permanent may have.
A word used to indicate a certain style of cost.
To give an unlocked designation to a permanent that has one or more locked halves.
One half of a split permanent is “unlocked” if it has the appropriate unlocked designation.
A permanent that becomes unprepared loses the prepared designation.
To rotate a permanent back to the upright position from a sideways position.
Part of the turn. This step is the first step of the beginning phase.
The untap symbol {Q} in an activation cost means “Untap this permanent.”
A default status a permanent may have.
Part of the turn. This step is the second step of the beginning phase.
1. A casual variant in which each player plays the role of a famous character. A card type seen only on nontraditional Magic cards in the Vanguard casual variant. A vanguard card is not a permanent.
An additional set of rules that determines the style of a multiplayer game.
An artifact subtype. Vehicles can become artifact creatures.
A variant of the venture into the dungeon ability that allows a player to bring a dungeon card with [quality] into the game or move a player’s venture marker.
A marker used to track which room of a dungeon card a player is currently in.

A Vibranium token is a colorless Vibranium artifact token with indestructible and “{T}: Add {C}. This mana can’t be spent to cast a nonartifact spell.” For more information about predefined tokens, see rule 111.10.
A Walker token is a 2/2 black Zombie creature token named Walker. For more information on predefined tokens, see rule 111.10.

A creature type with no particular rules meaning. Older cards with the Wall creature type but without defender had an unwritten ability that precluded them from attacking. Those cards have received errata in the Oracle card reference to have defender. Some older cards that referenced the Wall creature type have also received errata. See Defender.
There are several ways to win the game.
See Typecycling.
A supertype that’s normally relevant on enchantments.
A state-based action that causes all permanents with the world supertype except the one that has had the world supertype for the shortest amount of time are put into their owners’ graveyards.
A rules term used to describe a creature that’s legendary, not a Villain, and red and/or white.
A placeholder for a number that needs to be determined.
See X.
Words that refer to an object’s controller, its would-be controller (if a player is attempting to cast or activate it), or its owner (if it has no controller).
A place where objects can be during a game. See section 4, “Zones.”
Trigger events that involve objects changing zones.
